domains.title: Baekdusan, the White-Head Mountain
domains.subtitle: sacred volcano, origin mountain, and axis of the Korean world
domains.lead: Baekdusan is the sacred White-Head Mountain, a volcanic peak revered as an origin place, source of rivers, and spiritual axis in Korean and Manchu shamanism in Korean tradition. The name means "White head mountain" and belongs to the domain "Sacred Mountain, Origin." Baekdusan means "White-Head Mountain," named for the snow and pumice that cap its volcanic summit. It stands on the border of present-day China and North Korea and is the source of the Yalu (Amnok) and Tumen rivers.

cards.name: Sacred Peak
cards.desc: Baekdusan is one of the most revered mountains in the Korean cultural sphere.

cards.name: White-Head Mountain
cards.desc: Its snow-covered summit is a visible sign of purity and celestial proximity.

cards.name: Volcano of Origin
cards.desc: The mountain is tied to myths of cosmic and national beginnings.

cards.name: Border of Realms
cards.desc: Baekdusan marks a geopolitical boundary and a spiritual threshold.

symbols.name: Snow-capped peak
symbols.meaning: The white head that gives the mountain its name and signifies purity and height.

symbols.name: Lake Chonji
symbols.meaning: The crater lake at the summit, a mirror of heaven and a symbol of origin.

symbols.name: Tiger and bear
symbols.meaning: Animals of the mountain forests, echoing the Dangun myth of bear and tiger.

symbols.name: Pine tree
symbols.meaning: The hardy evergreen that clings to volcanic slopes and symbolises longevity.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Baekdusan is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Descent Place of Hwanung
myths.text: Some Korean traditions identify Baekdusan as the mountain where Hwanung descended from heaven beneath a sandalwood tree. From this sacred volcano the Korean people trace their origin and their connection to heaven.

myths.title: Baekdusan as Sansin
myths.text: Like other great mountains, Baekdusan is inhabited by a mountain spirit (sansin) who protects the land, grants visions to seekers, and serves as an intermediary between humans and heaven.

myths.title: The Ancestral Mountain
myths.text: Both Korean and Manchu shamanic traditions regard Baekdusan as an ancestral mountain and a source of spiritual power. Rituals and pilgrimages to the mountain sought blessings, healing, and contact with ancestral spirits.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 白 (baek, "white"), 頭 (du, "head"), and 山 (san, "mountain"). Read 백두산 in Korean, it describes the snow-covered volcanic peak that dominates the northern landscape.

nameVariations.note: Chinese name for the same mountain.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Baekdusan, the Hangul form is 백두산 and the Hanja form is 白頭山. Hangul ‘백두산’ and Hanja ‘白頭山’; the Chinese name is Changbai Shan, while Korean and Manchu traditions know it as a sacred ancestral mountain. The ASCII form baekdusan is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Baekdusan is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Baekdusan is a shared sacred site. Korean shamanism and national myth connect it to Hwanung and Dangun; Manchu shamanism treats it as an ancestral mountain; Chinese tradition knows it as Changbai Shan. Modern politics have layered nationalist meanings onto the peak, especially in North Korea, where it is central to state ideology. Religious pilgrimage, ecological conservation, and geopolitical dispute all converge on the mountain, making it one of the most symbolically charged landscapes in East Asia.
lore.culturalLegacy: Baekdusan occupies a unique place in Korean identity. It appears in poetry, painting, patriotic song, and North Korean state iconography. South Korean tourists undertake difficult pilgrimages to view the peak, and the mountain is a frequent subject of photography and documentary film. Environmental scientists study its volcanic crater lake, while shamans and Buddhist practitioners continue to honour it as a sacred mountain. The name itself has become shorthand for origin, purity, and national longing.
lore.extendedMeditation: Baekdusan invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
